question: In the lecture, it is argued that if a sequence \((X_N)\) is non‑negative and non‑decreasing from some index \(M_0\) onward, then it cannot converge to \(0\) unless all its terms from \(M_0\) onward are zero. Explain the logical reasoning that leads to this conclusion.

Taking \(\varepsilon = X_{M_0}\) (which is non‑negative), the monotonicity forces every later term to be at least \(X_{M_0}\). Thus if \(X_{M_0}>0\), all subsequent terms are \(\ge X_{M_0}>0\), contradicting the possibility that they become arbitrarily small. Therefore the only way the limit can be \(0\) is if \(X_{M_0}=0\), and by monotonicity this forces all later terms to be \(0\) as well. Hence, unless all terms from \(M_0\) onward are zero, the sequence cannot converge to \(0\).

question: In the lecture, the convergence of the alternating series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n x_n\) is examined. Explain why the requirement that \((x_n)\) is a monotone decreasing sequence converging to \(0\) guarantees convergence of this series, and describe how the proof strategy that first shows a convergent subsequence of partial sums leads to the convergence of the entire sequence of partial sums.  Additionally, contrast this situation with the case where \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n\) converges absolutely.
answer: The condition that \((x_n)\) is monotone decreasing and tends to \(0\) is precisely the hypothesis of the Alternating Series Test.  Because the terms decrease in magnitude and approach zero, the partial sums of the alternating series form two interlacing subsequences: the even partial sums \(S_{2k}\) and the odd partial sums \(S_{2k+1}\).  Each subsequence is monotone (the even ones are decreasing, the odd ones are increasing) and both are bounded (by the first term and by zero, respectively).  Hence each subsequence converges; let \(L_{\text{even}}\) and \(L_{\text{odd}}\) be their limits.  Since the difference between successive partial sums is \((-1)^{n+1}x_{n+1}\) and \(x_{n+1}\to0\), the two limits must coincide, so \(L_{\text{even}}=L_{\text{odd}}\).  Therefore the full sequence of partial sums converges to this common limit.  This argument mirrors the proof for \(p\)-series, where one first shows convergence of a convenient subsequence and then extends it to the whole sequence.\n\nIn contrast, if \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n\) converges absolutely (i.e., \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|\) converges), then the alternating series converges regardless of the sign pattern, and the convergence is unconditional.  Absolute convergence guarantees convergence of the series without needing the monotonicity or the alternating sign; the series of absolute values provides a dominating convergent series.  Thus, while the alternating series test gives conditional convergence under the monotonicity and limit‑to‑zero conditions, absolute convergence is a stronger property that ensures convergence even when the terms are not alternating.
